stem: A 51-year-old woman has had no menstrual bleeding for 9 months and has frequent night sweats. Which statement best describes her reproductive stage?

choices.text: She is postmenopausal because she has had more than 6 months of amenorrhea with vasomotor symptoms.
Her stage should be determined by a serum FSH level above 40 IU/L.
She is in the late menopause transition; menopause can be confirmed only after 12 months of amenorrhea.

rationale: Menopause is defined retrospectively by the final menstrual period after 12 months of amenorrhea. Amenorrhea of ≥60 days places her in the late transition (STRAW+10).

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Six months does not meet the 12-month criterion.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: STRAW+10 is anchored on bleeding pattern; FSH is supportive only and fluctuates.

learningObjective: Apply STRAW+10 menstrual criteria to stage the menopause transition.
author: AI draft

stem: Fezolinetant reduces vasomotor symptoms primarily by acting on which pathway?

choices.text: Blocking neurokinin B signaling at NK3 receptors on hypothalamic KNDy neurons
Inhibiting serotonin reuptake in the thermoregulatory center
Agonizing estrogen receptor-β in peripheral vasculature

rationale: Estrogen withdrawal leads to KNDy neuron hyperactivity and excess neurokinin B signaling to the thermoregulatory center. Fezolinetant is a selective NK3 receptor antagonist.

wrongAnswerRationales.c: VMS originate centrally; fezolinetant is not an estrogen receptor ligand.

learningObjective: Describe the KNDy mechanism underlying VMS and its pharmacologic target.
author: AI draft

stem: A 36-year-old woman has had 5 months of amenorrhea and hot flashes. Pregnancy test is negative. What is the most appropriate next step?

choices.text: Reassure her that early perimenopause is common and recheck in a year
Measure FSH and estradiol (repeated), with TSH and prolactin, to evaluate for primary ovarian insufficiency
Begin a salivary hormone panel to guide compounded therapy

rationale: Amenorrhea before 40 warrants evaluation for POI; laboratory testing is appropriate in this age group, unlike typical perimenopause after 45.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Menopause before 40 is not normal and needs evaluation.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Salivary testing is unreliable and compounded therapy is not recommended.

learningObjective: Recognize when laboratory evaluation is indicated in suspected POI.
author: AI draft

stem: Which statement about androgens in midlife women is correct?

choices.text: A total testosterone below the reference range confirms female androgen insufficiency.
Adrenal androgens decline abruptly at the final menstrual period.
No serum androgen concentration defines female androgen insufficiency, so levels should not guide diagnosis.

rationale: No serum androgen level defines female androgen insufficiency; checking levels to diagnose or guide treatment of low desire is not recommended.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Adrenal androgens rise moderately in the late transition and return toward baseline 1–2 years after the FMP.

learningObjective: Interpret the role of androgen testing in midlife women.
author: AI draft

stem: A 42-year-old woman undergoes bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for benign disease and declines estrogen. Compared with natural menopause, she is at increased risk of which long-term outcome?
rationale: Bilateral oophorectomy at or before 45 is associated with increased dementia and cardiovascular risk; estrogen until the average age of menopause appears to mitigate these risks.

wrongAnswerRationales.c: Hyperplasia relates to unopposed estrogen, not estrogen deficiency.

learningObjective: Identify health risks of early surgical menopause.
author: AI draft

stem: A 63-year-old woman using low-dose vaginal estradiol for 2 years reports one episode of light spotting. What is the best next step?

choices.text: Reassure her that spotting is expected with vaginal estrogen
Evaluate with transvaginal ultrasound and/or endometrial sampling
Add oral micronized progesterone and reassess in 6 months

rationale: Any postmenopausal bleeding warrants evaluation, regardless of vaginal estrogen use.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Bleeding should not be attributed to therapy without evaluation.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Progestogen is not indicated with low-dose vaginal ET and does not replace evaluation.

learningObjective: Manage postmenopausal bleeding in women using vaginal estrogen.
author: AI draft

stem: A 47-year-old woman who smokes a pack per day requests contraception and has heavy irregular bleeding. Which option is most appropriate?
rationale: Estrogen-containing contraception is inappropriate in a smoker over 35. The LNG-IUS provides contraception and treats heavy bleeding.
learningObjective: Select contraception in perimenopausal women with estrogen contraindications.
author: AI draft

stem: In which situation is serum FSH measurement most useful to assess menopausal status?

choices.text: A 49-year-old with a levonorgestrel IUD and new vasomotor symptoms
A 50-year-old with irregular cycles and hot flashes

rationale: Testing may help when bleeding cannot be used to assess status, such as with an LNG-IUD or after hysterectomy.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Clinical picture is sufficient; FSH fluctuates.

learningObjective: Identify appropriate indications for hormone testing.
author: AI draft

stem: Approximately what proportion of women with endometrial cancer present with abnormal uterine bleeding?
rationale: About 90% of women diagnosed with uterine cancer present with abnormal bleeding — the basis for evaluating all postmenopausal bleeding.
learningObjective: Recall the presentation of endometrial cancer.
author: AI draft

stem: A woman on continuous combined estrogen–progestogen therapy started 3 months ago reports irregular light bleeding. She has no other symptoms. What is the most appropriate approach?

choices.text: Counsel that unscheduled bleeding is common early; evaluate if it persists beyond about 6 months or is heavy

rationale: Unscheduled bleeding is common in the first months of continuous combined therapy; persistent bleeding beyond ~6 months warrants evaluation.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Not required this early for light bleeding without risk factors.

learningObjective: Manage expected bleeding patterns on EPT.
author: AI draft

stem: What proportion of women experience vasomotor symptoms for more than 10 years?
rationale: VMS last a mean of 7–9 years, and roughly one-third of women experience them for more than 10 years.
learningObjective: Counsel on expected VMS duration.
author: AI draft

stem: In nonhormone VMS trials, which patient characteristic is associated with a greater placebo response?
rationale: Women with more anxiety show a higher placebo response; placebo improvement rates range from 20% to 66%.
learningObjective: Interpret placebo effects in VMS trials.
author: AI draft

stem: A healthy 52-year-old, 1 year past her final period, has 10 moderate-to-severe hot flashes daily and no contraindications. What is the most effective treatment?
rationale: HT is the most effective treatment for VMS and has a favorable benefit–risk ratio in women <60 or within 10 years of menopause.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Supplements not recommended; no benefit over placebo.

learningObjective: Select first-line therapy for bothersome VMS in an appropriate candidate.
author: AI draft

stem: Which comorbidity is a recognized risk factor for more bothersome vasomotor symptoms?
rationale: Comorbidities associated with VMS include thyroid disease, diabetes, obstructive sleep apnea and chronic pain conditions.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Thyroid disease is a risk factor, but the euthyroid treated state is not the listed association.

learningObjective: Identify risk factors for VMS.
author: AI draft

stem: A woman asks whether regular exercise will reduce her hot flashes. Based on the 2023 nonhormone statement, how should you counsel her?

choices.text: Exercise is Level I recommended for VMS reduction.
Exercise is not recommended specifically for VMS, though it has broad health benefits.
Exercise worsens VMS and should be avoided.

rationale: Exercise, yoga and cooling techniques are Level II not recommended for VMS treatment; exercise remains beneficial for overall health.
learningObjective: Counsel accurately about lifestyle measures for VMS.
author: AI draft

stem: A 54-year-old with an intact uterus starts transdermal estradiol for VMS. Which addition is required?

choices.text: Annual endometrial biopsy without a progestogen
A progestogen (or LNG-IUS), unless using CEE with bazedoxifene

rationale: Systemic estrogen with an intact uterus requires endometrial protection with a progestogen, LNG-IUS (off-label), or a TSEC.
learningObjective: Ensure endometrial protection with systemic estrogen.
author: AI draft

stem: A 66-year-old woman has used estradiol and micronized progesterone since age 52 for VMS, which recur when she tries to stop. She is otherwise healthy. What is the most appropriate counseling?

choices.text: Continuation can be reasonable with shared decision-making and periodic reevaluation of benefits and risks.
She must discontinue HT because she is over 65.
Switch to compounded estriol to lower risk.

rationale: There are no data to support routine discontinuation at 65; longer use for documented indications such as persistent VMS can be appropriate with periodic reassessment.

wrongAnswerRationales.c: Compounded products are not recommended and not shown safer.

learningObjective: Counsel on HT duration beyond 65.
author: AI draft

stem: In the WHI estrogen-alone (CEE) arm, what was observed for breast cancer?

choices.text: Reduced incidence and reduced breast cancer mortality
No effect on incidence or mortality

rationale: CEE alone was associated with reduced breast cancer incidence that persisted at long-term follow-up, and reduced breast cancer mortality.
learningObjective: Distinguish breast cancer outcomes for ET vs EPT in WHI.
author: AI draft

stem: A 50-year-old with a BMI of 36 and migraine without aura has bothersome VMS. Which estrogen route is preferred?
rationale: Transdermal estradiol avoids first-pass hepatic effects and is associated with lower VTE and stroke risk in observational data; stable levels may also help migraine.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Oral route increases VTE risk relative to transdermal.

learningObjective: Choose route of HT based on risk factors.
author: AI draft

stem: Under the FDA class labeling changes for menopausal hormone therapy announced in 2025 and approved beginning February 2026, which boxed warning was retained?

choices.text: Endometrial cancer for systemic estrogen-alone products
Probable dementia for all systemic products
Breast cancer for all estrogen-containing products

rationale: Statements on cardiovascular disease, breast cancer and probable dementia were removed from the boxed warning; the endometrial cancer boxed warning was retained for systemic estrogen-alone products.

wrongAnswerRationales.c: Removed from the boxed warning; retained elsewhere in labeling.

learningObjective: Describe current FDA labeling for menopausal HT.
author: AI draft

stem: In WHI participants aged 50–59 at enrollment, what was the effect of hormone therapy on all-cause mortality?
rationale: In women aged 50–59, all-cause mortality was significantly reduced (HR ~0.69), supporting the favorable profile of early initiation.

wrongAnswerRationales.c: It was assessed in age-stratified analyses.

learningObjective: Recall age-stratified WHI mortality findings.
author: AI draft

stem: A 48-year-old on tamoxifen for ER-positive breast cancer has severe hot flashes. Which agent is most appropriate?

choices.text: Venlafaxine 37.5 mg daily, titrating as needed

rationale: Paroxetine and fluoxetine strongly inhibit CYP2D6, reducing conversion of tamoxifen to endoxifen. Venlafaxine has minimal CYP2D6 effect.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Strong CYP2D6 inhibitor and not recommended for VMS.

learningObjective: Choose a nonhormone agent compatible with tamoxifen.
author: AI draft

stem: Which intervention is Level I NOT recommended for vasomotor symptoms in the 2023 nonhormone position statement?
rationale: Paced respiration is not recommended (Level I). CBT and hypnosis are recommended (Level I).
learningObjective: Distinguish recommended from not-recommended mind–body interventions.
author: AI draft

stem: A woman starting fezolinetant asks about monitoring. Per the 2024 boxed warning, what is required?

choices.text: Hepatic tests at baseline, monthly for the first 3 months, then at 6 and 9 months

rationale: The FDA added a boxed warning for rare serious liver injury (Dec 2024), requiring hepatic labs at baseline, monthly × 3 months, then at months 6 and 9.
learningObjective: Recall safety monitoring for fezolinetant.
author: AI draft

stem: A 55-year-old with prior DVT has frequent night sweats that disrupt sleep. She prefers a medication taken once at night. Which is most appropriate?

choices.text: Gabapentin at bedtime, titrated toward 900 mg/day or higher as tolerated

rationale: Gabapentin (Level I) reduces VMS; bedtime dosing leverages sedation for VMS-related sleep disruption. Systemic HT is avoided after VTE.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Not recommended; less effective with more adverse effects.

learningObjective: Select nonhormone therapy for nocturnal VMS.
author: AI draft

stem: Which SSRI is FDA approved specifically for moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms?
rationale: Low-dose paroxetine salt 7.5 mg was the first nonhormone FDA-approved therapy for VMS.
learningObjective: Recall FDA-approved nonhormone VMS agents.
author: AI draft

stem: A 74-year-old woman with mild cognitive impairment has bothersome VMS. Which nonhormone agent should be avoided?
rationale: Oxybutynin is anticholinergic; long-term use may be associated with cognitive decline, particularly in older adults.
learningObjective: Recognize anticholinergic risk with oxybutynin.
author: AI draft

stem: A 60-year-old with an intact uterus starts the estradiol 2 mg vaginal ring (releasing ~7.5 µg/day) for GSM. Which is correct?

choices.text: A progestogen is required for endometrial protection.
This ring will also adequately treat her moderate VMS.
No progestogen is needed and routine endometrial surveillance is not recommended.

rationale: The low-dose estradiol ring is local therapy; no progestogen is indicated and asymptomatic surveillance is not recommended.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Applies to the systemic-dose estradiol acetate ring.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Low-dose local therapy does not treat VMS.

learningObjective: Differentiate local from systemic vaginal rings.
author: AI draft

stem: What is first-line therapy for mild genitourinary syndrome of menopause?

choices.text: Regular vaginal moisturizers plus lubricants with sexual activity

rationale: Nonhormone lubricants and long-acting moisturizers are first-line (Level A).

wrongAnswerRationales.c: Local therapy is preferred for isolated GSM.

learningObjective: Apply the GSM treatment ladder.
author: AI draft

stem: Which finding is typical of GSM on office testing?

choices.text: Vaginal pH below 4.5 with abundant lactobacilli
Vaginal pH greater than 5.0 with parabasal cells
Clue cells with positive whiff test

rationale: Hypoestrogenism raises vaginal pH (>5.0) and increases parabasal cells with reduced lactobacilli; these tests support but are not required for diagnosis.
learningObjective: Recognize objective findings in GSM.
author: AI draft

stem: A 58-year-old with moderate dyspareunia due to GSM declines all vaginal products. Which prescription option fits her preference?
rationale: Ospemifene is the only oral prescription option for moderate–severe dyspareunia due to menopause.
learningObjective: Select GSM therapy by route preference.
author: AI draft

stem: A 66-year-old has had three culture-proven UTIs in the past year and signs of vaginal atrophy. Which intervention has evidence to reduce recurrence?
rationale: Low-dose vaginal estrogen may prevent recurrent UTIs in postmenopausal women. Systemic HT has no urinary indication.
learningObjective: Manage recurrent UTI associated with GSM.
author: AI draft

stem: Systemic hormone therapy has what effect on stress urinary incontinence?

choices.text: It improves stress incontinence and is FDA approved for it.
It may worsen stress urinary incontinence.
It has no relationship to urinary symptoms.

rationale: Systemic HT does not improve urinary incontinence and may increase stress urinary incontinence.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: HT has no FDA urinary indication.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: An adverse association has been observed.

learningObjective: Recall urinary effects of systemic HT.
author: AI draft

stem: A 53-year-old with chronic insomnia but no VMS asks for a sleep treatment. What is first-line?
rationale: CBT-I is first-line for insomnia in menopausal women with durable benefit. No HT is FDA approved for insomnia.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Not indicated for insomnia without VMS.

learningObjective: Choose first-line insomnia therapy.
author: AI draft

stem: A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman has distressing low sexual desire. Her total testosterone is low-normal. How should HSDD be diagnosed?

choices.text: Clinically, based on history and distress, after addressing contributing factors
By total testosterone below the female reference range

rationale: HSDD is a clinical diagnosis. Serum testosterone should not be used to diagnose it; baseline testing is used to exclude high levels before therapy.
learningObjective: Diagnose HSDD appropriately.
author: AI draft

stem: Which statement about hormone therapy and cognition is correct?

choices.text: HT is recommended to prevent dementia if started within 10 years of menopause.
HT is not recommended at any age to prevent or treat cognitive decline or dementia.
HT reduces dementia when initiated after age 65.

rationale: HT is not recommended for cognitive indications at any age; initiation ≥65 increased dementia in WHIMS.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: The timing hypothesis does not create a dementia indication.

learningObjective: Counsel on HT and cognition.
author: AI draft

stem: A perimenopausal woman with a history of major depression has 3 weeks of depressed mood, anhedonia and poor sleep. What is first-line management?
rationale: Antidepressants and psychotherapy are first-line for MDD in midlife. Estrogen is not FDA approved for mood.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: May help some perimenopausal women but not first-line or approved.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Delays treatment of a major depressive episode.

learningObjective: Manage perimenopausal depression.
author: AI draft

stem: A woman on oral conjugated estrogens reports new low libido. Which change is most likely to help by a hormonal mechanism?
rationale: Oral estrogen increases SHBG and reduces bioavailable testosterone; transdermal estradiol has less effect on SHBG.

wrongAnswerRationales.c: Oral DHEA supplements are not recommended.

learningObjective: Recognize route effects on SHBG and libido.
author: AI draft

stem: A 58-year-old with a prior unprovoked PE has bothersome VMS. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

choices.text: A nonhormone therapy such as an SSRI/SNRI, gabapentin or an NK antagonist

rationale: With VTE history, systemic oral HT is contraindicated; nonhormone therapy is first-line. Low-dose transdermal therapy may be considered later with hematology input.
learningObjective: Manage VMS in women with VTE history.
author: AI draft

stem: Which is an FDA-approved indication for systemic hormone therapy?

choices.text: Primary prevention of coronary heart disease

rationale: HT is FDA approved for prevention of osteoporosis. It is not approved for CHD prevention; diabetes reduction is observed but not an indication.
learningObjective: Recall FDA-approved HT indications.
author: AI draft

stem: A 52-year-old whose mother and sister had VTE wants systemic HT. She has never had a clot. What is the best next step?

choices.text: Consider thrombophilia evaluation and favor transdermal therapy if HT is chosen
Start oral estrogen without further evaluation

rationale: A family history of VTE warrants consideration of thrombophilia evaluation; thrombophilia without prior VTE is a relative contraindication, and transdermal routes carry lower risk.

wrongAnswerRationales.c: It is a relative, not absolute, contraindication.

learningObjective: Assess thrombotic risk before HT.
author: AI draft

stem: A 68-year-old woman, 18 years postmenopause, with hypertension and dyslipidemia asks to start systemic HT to 'protect her heart.' What is the best response?

choices.text: HT is appropriate because it is cardioprotective at any age.
HT is not indicated for cardioprotection, and initiation this far from menopause carries higher absolute CV risk.
HT is appropriate if delivered transdermally.

rationale: HT has no CVD prevention indication; initiation >60 or >10 years from menopause carries higher absolute CHD, stroke and VTE risk.

wrongAnswerRationales.c: Route does not create a cardioprotective indication.

learningObjective: Counsel on HT and CVD prevention.
author: AI draft

stem: What degree of weight loss improves blood pressure, lipids, glucose and fatty liver in midlife women with obesity?

choices.text: Only weight loss to normal BMI

rationale: Modest weight loss of 3–10% improves metabolic parameters, fatty liver, chronic pain and CVD risk.
learningObjective: Counsel on benefits of modest weight loss.
author: AI draft

stem: A 70-year-old has received denosumab for 4 years and wants to stop. What is the most appropriate plan?

choices.text: Transition to a bisphosphonate to prevent rebound bone loss
Stop denosumab and recheck DXA in 2 years
Take a 1-year drug holiday, then restart

rationale: Stopping denosumab causes rebound bone turnover with rapid BMD loss and multiple vertebral fractures; follow-on therapy (usually a bisphosphonate) is needed.

wrongAnswerRationales.c: Holidays apply to bisphosphonates, not denosumab.

learningObjective: Manage denosumab discontinuation.
author: AI draft

stem: A 67-year-old has taken alendronate for 5 years. She has never fractured and her hip T-score is now −1.9. What is reasonable?

choices.text: Consider a bisphosphonate drug holiday with reassessment

rationale: A holiday can be considered after 3–5 years in low/moderate-risk patients who no longer meet treatment criteria, with monitoring.
learningObjective: Apply bisphosphonate holiday criteria.
author: AI draft

stem: A woman's femoral neck T-score improves from −2.7 to −2.3 on treatment. What is her diagnosis?
rationale: Once osteoporosis is diagnosed, improvement in T-score above −2.5 on therapy does not remove the diagnosis.
learningObjective: Interpret BMD changes on treatment.
author: AI draft

stem: What total daily calcium intake is recommended for postmenopausal women?
rationale: Total calcium ~1,200 mg/day, diet preferred; higher intake mostly from supplements is not recommended and increased kidney stones in WHI.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: 2,000 mg is the upper limit and supplements raise stone risk.

learningObjective: Recall calcium recommendations.
author: AI draft

stem: A 72-year-old has two recent vertebral compression fractures and a lumbar T-score of −3.6. Which sequence is most appropriate?

choices.text: An osteoanabolic agent first, followed by an antiresorptive

rationale: Very-high-risk patients benefit from anabolic therapy first, then an antiresorptive to maintain gains.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Nonpharmacologic measures do not substantially increase BMD.

learningObjective: Sequence therapy in very-high-risk osteoporosis.
author: AI draft

stem: A 57-year-old stopping HT after 6 years asks about her bones. What should you anticipate?

choices.text: BMD gains persist for at least 10 years
BMD declines toward pretreatment levels within 1–2 years; reassess fracture risk

rationale: After discontinuation of estrogen, BMD declines within 1–2 years; consider DXA and alternative therapy if at risk.
learningObjective: Plan bone care after stopping HT.
author: AI draft

stem: A 34-year-old with POI and no contraindications asks about hormone therapy. What is the best recommendation?

choices.text: HT at least until the average age of natural menopause (~52), possibly at higher-than-standard doses
Avoid HT because of WHI breast cancer findings
HT for 2 years only, then stop

rationale: Women with POI should receive HT at least until the average age of menopause unless contraindicated; WHI does not apply and higher doses may be needed.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: WHI did not include this population.

learningObjective: Manage HT in POI.
author: AI draft

stem: A 61-year-old on anastrozole for ER-positive breast cancer has severe dyspareunia despite 3 months of moisturizers and lubricants. What is the next step?

choices.text: Discuss low-dose vaginal estrogen or vaginal DHEA with her oncologist, with pelvic floor therapy and dilators as adjuncts

rationale: For GSM refractory to nonhormone measures, low-dose vaginal ET or DHEA may be considered with oncology after shared decision-making; AI users warrant extra caution.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Systemic HT is generally not advised.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Not approved in the US for women with a breast cancer history.

learningObjective: Manage GSM in breast cancer survivors.
author: AI draft

stem: A 40-year-old BRCA1 carrier without breast cancer had risk-reducing BSO and hysterectomy. She has severe VMS. What is most appropriate?

choices.text: Avoid HT because it negates the breast cancer risk reduction from surgery
Estrogen-alone therapy until about the average age of menopause

rationale: Observational data suggest BRCA carriers after RRBSO receive HT benefits with minimal to no increase in breast cancer risk; without a uterus, ET alone is used.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: HT does not appear to negate the risk reduction.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: No progestogen is needed without a uterus.

learningObjective: Counsel BRCA carriers after RRBSO.
author: AI draft

stem: Without atypia, the risk of endometrial hyperplasia progressing to cancer over 20 years is less than 5%. With atypia, the risk rises to approximately:
rationale: Hyperplasia with atypia carries ~28% progression risk vs <5% without atypia.
learningObjective: Recall progression risk of endometrial hyperplasia.
author: AI draft

stem: A survivor of early-stage, low-grade endometrial cancer has GSM that has not responded to moisturizers. Which is most appropriate?

choices.text: No hormonal therapy of any kind is permitted
Low-dose vaginal estrogen after discussion with her oncologist
Systemic estrogen-alone therapy as first choice

rationale: For select endometrial cancer survivors who fail nonhormone therapy, low-dose vaginal ET appears safe in observational data and improves quality of life.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Too restrictive for low-grade, early-stage disease.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Local therapy is preferred for isolated GSM.

learningObjective: Manage GSM in endometrial cancer survivors.
author: AI draft
